text:
CMakeLists.txt

Code file CMakeLists.txt
# Minimum CMake version required
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.10)

# Project name and version
project(Example VERSION 1.0)

# Set the C++ standard
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED True)

# Add the include directory for headers
include_directories(${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/include)

# Add the static library
add_library(math_utils STATIC src/math_utils.cpp)

# Add the executable
add_executable(main src/main.cpp)

# Link the static library to the executable
target_link_libraries(main PRIVATE math_utils)

target_compile_options(main PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)

Additional lines CMakeLists.txt
# Add Cppcheck as a custom target
find_program(CMAKE_CXX_CPPCHECK NAMES cppcheck)
if (CMAKE_CXX_CPPCHECK)
    add_custom_target(
        cppcheck
        COMMAND ${CMAKE_CXX_CPPCHECK}
        --enable=all
        --inconclusive
        --std=c++${CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD}
        --quiet
        --suppress=missingIncludeSystem
        --output-file=${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/cppcheck_report.txt
        ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/src
        ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/include
        ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/tests
        COMMENT "Running Cppcheck static analysis..."
        VERBATIM
    )
else()
    message(WARNING "Cppcheck not found! Static analysis will not be available.")
endif()

text:
Copy constructor 2/3

Function foo creates a new object aFoo and copies all values from a.
We did not specify how this new class A is copied!
By default all variables are simply copied. I.e., aFoo._d = a._d.
aFoo is deallocated when leaving function (static memory!)
Destructor of aFoo deallocates aFoo._d and thereby a._d.
Good thing we understand pointers ;)

Way out: Define our own copy constructor.

text:
A simple stencil code
Python
for i in np.arange(1, N - 1):
  for j in np.arange(1, N - 1):
      out[j + i * N] = inn[j + i * N] \
                     + alpha * (inn[j - 1 + i * N] - 
                               2.0 * inn[j + i * N] + inn[j + 1 + i * N])

Compile and Wall time (2nd order):  7.65 s (1.08 s with numba)
                                           (0.67 s with slicing)
C++

for(int i = 1; i < N-1; i++)
    for(int j = 1; j < N-1; j++)
        out[j + i * N] = in[j + i * N] 
                       + alpha * (in[j - 1 + i * N] - 
                                 2.0 * in[j + i * N] + in[j + 1 + i * N]);

Compile and Wall time (2nd order): 0.28 s

title: 1. Why we teach C++ and some basics
text:
Performance implications

Drastic performance improvement (\(\approx 27\)x).

Reduces run time for your code.

Python is an interpreted language.

A program, the interpreter, reads the python code and executes one statement after another.

C++ is a compiled language that uses a two-step approach

Compilation: A program, the compiler, reads the C++ code and translates it into machine code.
Execution: The machine code is directly executed by the CPU.


🤓: In reality Python uses an intermediate representation (bytecode) and relies on compiled Fortran/C/C++ code.

title: 1. Why we teach C++ and some basics
text:
What is compilation
Can we compile Python?
x = 3           # x is a integer
if condition:
    x = 3.0     # x is a floating point number
y = 2 * x

What operation should 2 * x be compiled to?

integer/floating point multiplication

Compiler would need to understand all possible types that x can have.

For an interpreted language this is much simpler (can be decided during run time)

In C++ type information need to be specified at compile time.

Having type information available makes optimizing the machine code easier.

title: 1. Why we teach C++ and some basics
1. Why we teach C++ and some basics
section: Performance and use of the language
text:
Performance and use of the language
In Python using the second order method is \(1.5\)x faster than fourth order method. In C++ the second and fourth order methods take the same time.

Performance is often limited by fetching data from memory and not by the number of arithmetic operations the CPU can perform. This is called a memory bound problem.

Writing Python code to predict the performance of a C++ code is a bad idea!
Why is Python used?: Many software packages have embraced a high-level Python interface.
Python is often used to specify the problem but all the heavy lifting is done under the hood is usually in C++.
Makes the software approachable for users while maintaining good performance.

Whenever possible, we would like to tell the program how many bits we need.
Remember that the C++ compiler requires us to define the type in advance
x = 3 # x is a integer
if condition:
  x = 3.0 # x is a floating point number
y = 2 * x
Types simplify readability.
Main types are: char, string, int, long, float, double

title: 1. Why we teach C++ and some basics
text:
Code example

Code file main_typer.cpp
int main() {
  int i;          // declaration
  i = 2;          // definition
  float d = 2.3f; // declaration and definition
  double a = 1.0, b = 2.3;
  return 0;
}

From the code, the compiler knows that:

\(16\) bit are needed for i,
\(32\) bit for d,
\(64\) for a and b.

It is good practice to declare variables at the beginning of the code.

text:
Compiler and linker basics

We write code that humans understand but computers can’t → translation into machine language
The main tools are the compiler and the linker.
Compiler: C++ code into machine language file (object file, main.o, main.obj)
Linker: combine obj files and libraries (precompiled code)
$ g++ -c hello.cpp
$ g++ -o hello.out hello.o
$ ls
hello.cpp  hello.o  hello.out
We will revisit the compiler multiple times once our programs become more complicated.

text:
🏆 Advanced Exercise

Solving an ordinary differential equation
Consider a simple ODE \[
\dot y(t) = \sin(y(t))
\]
Forward Euler time discretization: Define grid \(\{t_1,\cdots,t_{N}\}\) and define \(y^n \simeq y(t_n)\) \[
    y^{n+1} = y^{n} + (t_{n+1}-t_n) \sin(y^n)
\]
Implement a forward Euler method with equidistant time step size \(\Delta t = t_{n+1}-t_n = 0.01\). Store the solution at all time points \(t\in[0, 1]\) in a vector and write it to a text file.

title: 2. Memory Management
text:
Multi-dimensional arrays
In the C/C++ standard there is no dynamic multi-dimensional array.

option: Use a pointer to a pointer.

Access via a[i][j].

Not very good memory layout on modern computer architectures (pointer chasing).


option: Use an one-dimensional array and do the index calculations by hand.

Access via a[i + j*n].

option: Use an external library that implements 2d arrays.

Access is usually provided by a(i, j)

text:
Linter
Why does it make sense to use a Linter?

In C/C++ the control flow is done via { ... }
The compiler does not care how it is formatted but we should, it is easier

to navigate the code
to find bugs
to maintain the code
to homogenise styles between different people

We use such tools to have consistent code style/coding standard in the project
It allows to check for (common) problems → clean-up before a commit

Static code analysis like unreachable code
assigned but never used
syntax errors
vulnerabilities
undefined or dangerous behaviour

title: 3. Libraries
text:
Libraries
Similar to other programming languages in C++ we do not write everything ourself. Therefore, libraries are linked during the build.

Static library: contains code that is linked to our program at compile time. The code is copied into our executable.
Dynamic/shared library: contains code shared by multiple programs. The code is loaded at runtime and shared over multiple executables.




Types of libraries

title: 3. Libraries
text:
Libraries
Similar to other programming languages in C++ we do not write everything ourself. Therefore, libraries are linked during the build.

Static library: contains code that is linked to our program at compile time. The code is copied into our executable.
Dynamic/shared library: contains code shared by multiple programs. The code is loaded at runtime and shared over multiple executables.




Libraries in memory

title: 3. Libraries
text:
Pros and cons 1/2









Feature
Static Libraries
Dynamic Libraries




Linking
At compile time
At runtime


Executable Size
Larger (library code is included)
Smaller (only references to the library)


Code Sharing
No
Yes (shared across multiple programs)


Runtime Dependency
None (self-contained executable)
Requires the library to be present at runtime


Performance
Faster (no runtime loading)
Slightly slower (runtime loading overhead)

title: 3. Libraries
text:
Pros and cons 2/2









Feature
Static Libraries
Dynamic Libraries




Updates
Requires recompilation of the executable
Can update the library without recompiling


Deployment
Easier (single executable)
More complex (library must be distributed)


Memory Usage
Higher (duplicate copies in memory)
Lower (shared library in memory)


Debugging
Easier (all code is in the executable)
Harder (external dependencies to track)


Security
Safer (no external library tampering)
Risk of library hijacking or tampering

title: 3. Libraries
3. Libraries
text:
Compiling


Static library
# compile the library to an object file
$ g++ -c math_utils.cpp -o math_utils.o
# bundle object into static library
$ ar rcs libmath_utils.a math_utils.o
# Compile
$ g++ -I. -c main.cpp -o main.o
$ g++ -L. main.o libmath_utils.a -o main
# alternative
$ g++ main.o -L. -lmath_utils -o main.out
# run th executable
./main.out

Dynamic library
# compile the library to an object file
$ g++ -c math_utils.cpp -o math_utils.o
# bundle object(s) into shared library
$ g++ -shared -o libmath_utils.so math_utils.o
# Compile
$ g++ -I. -c main.cpp -o main.o
$ g++ -L. main.o libmath_utils.so -o main.out
# alternative
$ g++ main.o -L. -lmath_utils -o main.out
# Specify location of shared library
$ export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$LD_LIBRARY_PATH:./
# run the executable
$ ./main.out
